title: Warnings Are Visible But Their Meaning Is Unclear
summary: This failure occurs when a warning is present and noticed, but the user cannot immediately understand what condition it describes, how urgent it is, or what response it requires. The source evidence covers text-based warnings in surgical use, colour-only warning channels, contextual detachment on an e-bike display, and related alarm and status-comprehension cases.
keyFacts: The failure is not warning absence; the warning is present but its meaning is not immediately accessible.
A warning that interrupts the task but does not communicate actionable meaning produces confusion rather than response.
Text-label warnings are structurally weak in brief-glance environments because reading requires sequential processing and sustained attention.
Colour-only warning systems are vulnerable when lighting, glare, night-vision conditions, or colour perception reduce reliable colour discrimination.
Warning content can fail when it uses technical error codes, diagnostic descriptions, or status paragraphs that require interpretation before action.
Warnings can become unclear when they appear detached from the screen context or system state that gives them meaning.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, Creative Navy used twelve human factors studies and ergonomics papers, thirteen structured sessions with eight surgeons, and benchmarking of six comparable surgical instruments.
In structured deSoutter review sessions, eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons reported that device state, including warning states, could be verified during brief glances without reading.

In the Stromer e-bike testing before redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention; after redesign, warnings did not appear on the issues list, and the same result remained two years later.
Creative Navy's documented design standard for warning states was that no critical warning should rely on colour alone or require reading to interpret.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Warning-Meaning Failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A warning-meaning failure occurs when an interface presents a warning that is visible but not immediately interpretable for the user, task, environment, and time available. The user may see the warning, recognise that the system is signalling something, and still be unable to determine the condition, urgency, or required response quickly enough for the operating context.

This is an interpretation failure. It is different from a warning that is absent, hidden, or not noticed. It is also different from a warning that is understood but not actionable. In this failure, the warning has been encountered, but its meaning is not immediately recoverable.

bodySections.heading: Warnings Can Interrupt the Task Without Reducing Uncertainty
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A warning that is not understood can draw attention away from the primary task while failing to provide actionable meaning. The operational cost is the combination of interruption and uncertainty: the user is pulled away from current work and required to interpret the system state at the moment when the warning should have reduced ambiguity.

This pattern appears when a text-label warning must be read during a live procedure, when a technical error code is combined with a paragraph of status description, when warning colour is unreliable under variable lighting, or when an embedded-display alert appears without enough surrounding context for the user to understand what it refers to.

The design problem is therefore not only whether the warning is visible. The warning must communicate meaning quickly enough for the attention, time, and environmental constraints of the situation in which it appears.

bodySections.heading: How Warning Meaning Becomes Unclear in Interfaces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Warnings become unclear when the warning channel does not match the conditions of use. Text may be adequate when users can read with sustained attention, but it is weak when users work through brief glances while attending to a patient, a road, a physical process, or a high-throughput operational flow.

Warnings also become unclear when colour is the sole differentiating cue. Colour can be efficient and salient under favourable display and lighting conditions, but it becomes fragile when glare, variable lighting, night-vision equipment, or colour-perception differences reduce reliable discrimination.

Warning content can be visible and technically correct while still requiring too much interpretation. A technical error code, diagnostic message, or internally oriented status description may state what the system knows, while failing to state what the user needs to recognise.

Warnings can also be contextually detached. The message may be legible, but the current screen may not show the state, component, or workflow condition that gives the warning meaning.

bodySections.heading: Text Warnings Are Weak in Brief-Glance Environments
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Text-label warnings fail when the operating context does not provide enough time or attention for reading. Reading requires sequential processing: the user must read words in order, hold earlier words in working memory, and integrate the sequence into meaning. Under brief-glance conditions, that process may not complete.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical-device case illustrates this mechanism. The Zethon bone cutter is a powered ultrasonic surgical instrument used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery. Surgeons operate the interface during live procedures, with primary attention on the surgical field and the patient, through gloves, under operating theatre lighting, and within sterile-field constraints.

In that context, text-label warnings created a use-related risk under IEC 62366-1 if sustained attention had to be diverted from the surgical field, and a different use-related risk if the warning was not understood. Creative Navy's design response shifted critical warning interpretation from reading to recognition through fixed spatial position, distinct icon form, and reserved colour semantics applied exclusively to warning states.

bodySections.heading: Colour Must Be Redundant, Not the Sole Warning Channel
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Colour-only warning systems fail when colour is treated as the semantic channel rather than as one redundant cue. A colour distinction can be perceptible under ideal conditions and unreliable under real operating conditions.

Creative Navy's benchmarking for the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement covered six comparable surgical instruments, including powered saws, ultrasonic tools, and other high-speed instruments used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery. The common pattern across the benchmarked devices was reliance on colour coding and text labels, without a recognisable pattern system that allowed state to be confirmed without reading.

The design response is not to remove colour. The design response is to make colour redundant. Spatial position, icon form, and colour should each contribute to the same warning state, so that degradation of any one channel does not make the warning uninterpretable.

bodySections.heading: Warning Content Should Support Recognition Before Diagnosis
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Warning content fails when it is written for internal diagnosis rather than user action under time pressure. A technical error code may be accurate, and a status description may correctly identify what has happened, but the warning still fails if the user must decode it before knowing whether to stop, continue, or change the current action.

This failure is common when warning content is shaped by engineering-centric documentation needs. The warning captures what the system knows, but in a form that serves technical completeness rather than operational response.

A more robust warning pattern communicates urgency and implied response through form before technical detail. Progressive disclosure can place the actionable interpretation first and keep diagnostic detail available as a secondary layer for users who need it.

bodySections.heading: Contextual Detachment Makes Visible Warnings Hard to Understand
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Warnings become contextually detached when they appear without the screen state, workflow state, or component relationship needed to understand them. The user may recognise that a warning exists, but may not be able to connect it to the current task without navigating elsewhere or already knowing what the message refers to.

The Stromer e-bike embedded-display case illustrates this failure. Stromer manufactures premium e-bikes whose embedded display is used while riding. The rider reads the display in brief glances while attention remains on the road.

Before Creative Navy's engagement, warnings had been layered onto an existing screen architecture after earlier design work by another provider. Creative Navy's structured testing before the redesign found that riders encountered warnings and recognised that something was being communicated, but could not recover the meaning without navigating away from the current context. During a ride, that action was not reliably available and was not safe.

Creative Navy's redesign addressed the warning system at the architectural level, including the layout and overlay system, the information architecture, and the contextual grounding of warning types.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Warning Interpretation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses warning interpretation failure by establishing when and how warnings will be encountered under real operating conditions before warning forms are specified. Domain learning determines the workflow moment, attention state, physical environment, and available time for interpretation.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, Creative Navy's domain learning involved twelve human factors studies and ergonomics papers, thirteen structured sessions with eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons, and benchmarking of six comparable surgical instruments. The design standard that emerged required warning states to be interpretable through pattern recognition in a brief glance, without reading, under variable theatre lighting, and through redundant cues.

In the Stromer engagement, Creative Navy's domain learning treated the previous design work as an accelerated first iteration. The analysis identified that the screen architecture and warning system had been designed separately, producing warnings that appeared without the contextual information required for immediate interpretation.

bodySections.heading: Scope Boundaries for This Failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
This page concerns warnings whose meaning is unclear. It does not cover warnings that are absent, hidden, or not noticed. It also does not cover the related failure in which warnings are visible and understood but the interface does not provide a clear path to action.

The relevant design question is whether the warning can be interpreted under the real conditions in which it appears: the user's available attention, the physical environment, the screen context, the time available for response, and the reliability of the channels used to communicate urgency and meaning.

strongClaims: A warning-meaning failure occurs when a warning is present and visible but its condition, urgency, or required response is not immediately recoverable under the conditions of use.
Text-label warnings are inadequate in brief-glance environments because reading requires sequential processing and sustained attention that may not be available during the primary task.
Colour-only warning differentiation is fragile under variable lighting, glare, night-vision conditions, and colour-perception differences.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, Creative Navy designed critical warning states using fixed spatial position, distinct icon form, and reserved colour, with no critical state relying on colour alone or requiring reading.

In Stromer testing before redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention; after redesign and again two years later, warnings did not appear on the issues list.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses warning interpretation failure through domain learning and by evaluating warning states against the real conditions in which they will be encountered.
weakerClaims: Eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons in structured review sessions reported that device state, including warning states, could be verified during brief glances without reading.

Additional evidence from Oceaneering, Raymarine, an industrial automation audit, and the MDU shows related warning, alarm, and status-comprehension mechanisms, but each has a distinct evidence class and limitation.
limitations: This page covers warning interpretation failure, not warning absence and not the separate failure where a warning is understood but no action path is available.
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon outcomes are surgeon-reported from structured review sessions, not post-deployment operational measurements.

Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail structured to support IEC 62366-1 verification and validation activities in the deSoutter engagement; summative validation was the manufacturer's responsibility, and compliance was not delivered as an outcome by Creative Navy.
The Stromer results come from Creative Navy-designed and run structured testing under real riding conditions; the source does not describe independent replication.
Oceaneering evidence is interview-sourced and specification-based; no operator was interviewed, no depot was visited, and nothing was measured.
Raymarine findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture, not radio performance, real-world calling accuracy, or outcomes at sea.

The industrial automation evidence is an audit finding about a product in development for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells; it is not a general claim about industrial software.
The MDU alarm model describes design decisions and advisor reasoning for comfort, cargo, and crew-safety alarms; no alarm-response figure or safety outcome is attached.
